st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Starr accepts selective, human-led deployment rather than wholesale substitution: he recognises useful bounded applications but excludes current systems from legal briefing absent demonstrated reliability. He materially extends the cluster’s verification and governance proposition through a mandatory human-checking certificate, continuing Rule 11 responsibility and a case-specific route to permission.
qs: All attorneys appearing before the Court must file on the docket a certificate attesting either that no portion of the filing was drafted by generative artificial intelligence (such as ChatGPT, Harvey.AI, or Google Bard) or that any language drafted by generative artificial intelligence was checked for accuracy, using print reporters or traditional legal databases, by a human being.
Any party believing a platform has the requisite accuracy and reliability for legal briefing may move for leave and explain why.

kp.k: Starr requires certification of nonuse or human accuracy checking
kp.d: The court text archived 31 May 2023 requires all attorneys appearing before Judge Starr to certify either that no filing language was drafted by generative AI or that a human checked AI-drafted language using print reporters or traditional legal databases. It expressly includes ChatGPT, Harvey.AI and Google Bard. Legal Dive reports that the template covers quotations, citations, paraphrased assertions and legal analysis. This is a judge-specific verification requirement rather than an unconditional prohibition on AI-assisted filings.
qs: All attorneys appearing before the Court must file on the docket a certificate attesting either that no portion of the filing was drafted by generative artificial intelligence (such as ChatGPT, Harvey.AI, or Google Bard) or that any language drafted by generative artificial intelligence was checked for accuracy, using print reporters or traditional legal databases, by a human being.
Starr’s order about legal filings drafted by generative AI covers quotations, citations, paraphrased assertions and legal analysis, according to a template certificate posted online.

kp.k: The reproduced version expands coverage and specifies certification timing
kp.d: The Texas EnRLS reproduction, citing a court page last visited 7/24/2024, differs from the archived 2023 text: it expressly includes pro se litigants, requires the certificate together with the notice of appearance, and frames the assurance prospectively for any filing. These textual differences should not be collapsed into a single version or treated as evidence of a specified amendment date.
qs: All attorneys and pro se litigants appearing before the Court must, together with their notice of appearance, file on the docket a certificate attesting either that no portion of any filing will be drafted by generative artificial intelligence (such as ChatGPT or Harvey.AI) or that any language drafted by generative artificial intelligence will be checked for accuracy, using print reporters or traditional legal databases, by a human being

kp.k: Starr distinguishes useful legal tasks from reliable legal briefing
kp.d: Starr acknowledges potential uses in form divorces, discovery requests, document error identification and oral-argument preparation, while asserting that platforms in their then-current states are unsuitable for legal briefing because of hallucinations and bias. The order supplies no measured error rates or comparative performance study. It allows parties to seek leave by explaining a platform’s accuracy and reliability.
qs: These platforms are incredibly powerful and have many uses in the law: form divorces, discovery requests, suggested errors in documents, anticipated questions at oral argument. But legal briefing is not one of them.
These platforms in their current states are prone to hallucinations and bias. On hallucinations, they make stuff up—even quotes and citations.
Any party believing a platform has the requisite accuracy and reliability for legal briefing may move for leave and explain why.

kp.k: Starr grounds reliability concerns in absent professional allegiance
kp.d: The order argues that attorneys’ sworn obligations distinguish them from generative systems and their programmers. Starr presents the absence of allegiance to clients, law and truth as a reason for distrust alongside bias concerns. This is the court’s stated professional-accountability rationale, not an empirical finding about the prevalence or sources of model bias.
qs: While attorneys swear an oath to set aside their personal prejudices, biases, and beliefs to faithfully uphold the law and represent their clients, generative artificial intelligence is the product of programming devised by humans who did not have to swear such an oath.
As such, these systems hold no allegiance to any client, the rule of law, or the laws and Constitution of the United States (or, as addressed above, the truth).

kp.k: AI drafting does not transfer responsibility away from attorneys
kp.d: The archived Starr order states that filings will be struck when an attorney fails to file the required certificate acknowledging the judge-specific requirements and Rule 11 responsibility. Attorneys remain responsible for signed and submitted content regardless of AI involvement. Legal Dive separately describes potential Rule 11 sanctions; the document does not report sanctions imposed by Starr under this requirement.
qs: Accordingly, the Court will strike any filing from an attorney who fails to file a certificate on the docket attesting that the attorney has read the Court’s judge-specific requirements and understands that he or she will be held responsible under Rule 11 for the contents of any filing that he or she signs and submits to the Court, regardless of whether generative artificial intelligence drafted any portion of that filing.

kp.k: Avianca litigation supplies a concrete example of unverified fabrication
kp.d: Lyle Moran’s Legal Dive coverage, published 1 June 2023, situates Starr’s directive amid attention to Steven A. Schwartz’s use of ChatGPT for research without independent verification. It reports six fake cases in a brief filed on his client’s behalf and potential sanctions in the pending Southern District of New York personal-injury litigation against Avianca. This is a reported incident, not a measured model error rate or a report of sanctions already imposed.
qs: Attorney Steven A. Schwartz utilized ChatGPT to conduct his legal research in a federal case without independently verifying its work, and a brief filed on his client’s behalf ultimately
cited six fake cases
in an ongoing personal injury lawsuit filed by his client against the Colombian airline Avianca pending in the Southern District of New York.

kp.k: Baylson requires disclosure and certification of every citation
kp.d: The Texas EnRLS sampling reproduces Judge Michael Baylson’s requirement for attorneys and pro se parties to disclose AI use in preparing papers filed in cases assigned to him and certify every citation to law or the record as accurate. Unlike Starr’s nonuse-or-verification certificate, the quoted Baylson requirement expressly demands disclosure when AI has been used in any way in preparing the filing.
qs: If any attorney for a party, or a pro se party, has used Artificial Intelligence (“AI”) in the preparation of any complaint, answer, motion, brief, or other paper, filed with the Court, and assigned to Judge Michael M. Baylson, MUST, in a clear and plain factual statement, disclose that AI has been used in any way in the preparation of the filing, and CERTIFY, that each and every citation to the law or the record in the paper, has been verified as accurate.

kp.k: Kang requires AI identification, records and checks against fabrication
kp.d: The sampling quotes Magistrate Judge Peter Kang requiring AI-created or AI-drafted text to be identified through the document’s title or caption, a preceding table, or a contemporaneous notice. Counsel must retain records identifying affected passages if requested. The order prohibits fictitious citations and uncorroboratable legal or factual assertions, and makes failure to check AI-produced citations or factual assertions grounds for potential sanctions.
qs: Counsel shall maintain records sufficient to identify, if requested by the Court, those portions of the text of a pleading, brief, or document submitted to the Court which was created or drafted by an AI tool.

Parties and counsel shall not file or otherwise present to the Court any briefs, pleadings, materials, other documents, or argument which contain AI-hallucinated citations to law, case or legal citations which are fictitious or nonexistent, or any uncorroboratable assertions of law or fact.

A pro se party or a counsel’s failure to confirm or double-check the accuracy, veracity, or even existence of a case or legal citation (or assertion of fact) created by an AI tool is grounds for potential sanctions.

kp.k: Fuentes requires tool-specific disclosure and personal review of authorities
kp.d: Legal Dive reports that Magistrate Judge Gabriel Fuentes updated his civil standing order to require disclosure of generative AI used for research or drafting, including the particular tool and manner of use. His quoted order treats personal reading and analysis of cited authorities as an existing Rule 11 expectation that continues despite AI adoption. The coverage says the AI section references both Starr’s requirement and the Schwartz incident.
qs: Any party using any generative AI tool to conduct legal research or to draft documents for filing with the Court must disclose in the filing that AI was used, with the disclosure including the specific AI tool and the manner in which it was used,

Just as the Court did before the advent of AI as a tool for legal research and drafting, the Court will continue to presume that the Rule 11 certification is a representation by filers, as living, breathing, thinking human beings, that they themselves have read and analyzed all cited authorities to ensure that such authorities actually exist and that the filings comply with Rule 11(b)(2),

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Judge Brantley Starr identifies useful legal applications for generative AI but regards its then-current reliability as unsuitable for unchecked legal briefing.
pts.d: Starr names form divorces, discovery requests, document-error suggestions and anticipated oral-argument questions as useful applications. He attributes briefing risks to fabricated quotations and citations, bias and the absence of the professional commitments borne by lawyers. These are present-state assessments, not predictions of lawyer displacement or market restructuring. Despite the categorical statement about briefing, the operative requirement permits AI-drafted language when a human checks its accuracy using print reporters or traditional legal databases.

pts.k: Starr's order makes human verification and certification conditions of AI-assisted filing while retaining the signer's Rule 11 responsibility.
pts.d: The archived May 2023 order requires attorneys to certify either that no filing language was AI-drafted or that AI-drafted language was checked by a human against specified sources. Starr states that filings will be struck for failure to file the required certificate. Responsibility for signed submissions remains with the attorney regardless of AI involvement. This establishes a supervised-use workflow rather than transferring responsibility to an AI system.

pts.k: The supplementary orders impose differing disclosure, verification and recordkeeping requirements on AI-assisted litigation work.
pts.d: Judge Michael Baylson requires disclosure of AI use in preparing filings and certification that every citation to law or the record has been verified. Magistrate Judge Peter Kang requires identification of AI-drafted submissions, counsel's retention of records identifying AI-created portions, and accuracy checks backed by potential sanctions. Magistrate Judge Gabriel Fuentes requires disclosure of the tool and its use for research or drafting and reiterates that human filers must read and analyze cited authorities. These requirements belong to the respective judges, not to Legal Dive reporter Lyle Moran.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The document supplies judicial requirements and a reported fabrication incident, but no benchmark data or measured error rates.
pts.d: Starr's order itself establishes the certification requirement and its stated enforcement consequence. His capability and bias assessments are supported by judicial reasoning rather than empirical tests; the comparison between lawyers' oaths and AI programming is an argument about professional responsibility. Moran's 1 June 2023 reporting supplies a concrete illustration: Steven A. Schwartz used ChatGPT for unverified legal research, and a brief filed for his client cited six fake cases in the Avianca litigation. At that reporting date, sanctions were described as potential, not already imposed. This incident is not a measurement of hallucination frequency and does not establish tool-specific performance for Harvey AI or Bard.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Starr's assessment is expressly about then-current platforms; the document contains distinct versions of his requirements and a route to seek leave based on reliability.
pts.d: The primary order is archived 31 May 2023, and the Legal Dive article is dated 1 June 2023. Starr qualifies his risk assessment with 'in their current states' and permits a party to move for leave by explaining a platform's accuracy and reliability for briefing. The Texas EnRLS reproduction, whose source link is marked last visited 24 July 2024, differs from the archived version: it expressly covers pro se litigants, requires certification with the notice of appearance, and uses prospective language about filings. The supplied text does not establish the effective date of those changes. None of these passages supplies a forecast date for reliable autonomous legal briefing.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The direct effects concern litigating attorneys, self-represented parties and the courts receiving their filings, rather than legal-market segments generally.
pts.d: Attorneys before Starr must provide certification and ensure human verification of AI-drafted language; noncompliance risks striking their filings, and AI use does not remove Rule 11 responsibility. The later reproduction expressly extends coverage to pro se litigants. Baylson, Kang and Fuentes impose their own judge-specific obligations on covered filers. Clients are indirectly affected when filings made on their behalf contain fabricated authorities or face procedural consequences. Fuentes frames fabricated legal research as a threat to the mission of federal courts. The document does not claim effects on law-firm staffing, pricing, ALSP competition or access to justice.
